title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied in higher education, how the field has developed over time, what ethical issues are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being used. Rather than testing one intervention, it systematically reviews 146 peer-reviewed articles published between 2007 and 2018 from Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO Education Source.

The review organizes AI uses into four broad application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. Across the included studies, the main users were undergraduate students, with a smaller number of studies on postgraduate students and institutional/administrative users. The paper notes that most studies are quantitative and that many use machine learning for prediction tasks, automated feedback, or tutoring support.

The authors conclude that AI research in higher education is growing quickly, but it is dominated by technical and quantitative work, with relatively little involvement from educators and very limited critical reflection on ethical implications such as privacy, costs, and possible workforce impacts. They also argue that many studies are short-term and often lack longitudinal evidence, so stronger pedagogical and ethical frameworks are needed for future AI applications in higher education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of higher-education AI research, not an empirical study of an intervention’s effects on learners. It synthesizes descriptive patterns and prior studies but does not present a direct evaluation with study-level causal evidence for the target comparison topic.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact estimate on middle school mathematics achievement, delayed retention, or subgroup effects. Its contribution is conceptual and bibliographic for higher education AI, so it does not provide measurable impact relevant to the retrieval topic.
